Official Week 3 Objectives

1. Describe the importance of glycolysis in the erythrocyte, including regulation of hemoglobin affinity and structural integrity.
2. Explain the clinical significance of anaerobic glycolysis.
3. Explain the basis of symptoms arising from glycolytic enzyme deficiency.
4. Describe the outcome of deficient gluconeogenesis resulting from excess ethanol or genetic defects.
5. Identify symptoms of glycogen storage diseases and explain their underlying causes.

Slides 3–10: Glycolysis in RBCs & Clinical Significance

Slide 4. Glucose-6-phosphate is shown as a metabolic crossroads: glycolysis, glycogen, the pentose-phosphate pathway, and glycan/glycolipid synthesis all branch from this node.
Slide 5. The glycolysis overview highlights the ten-step pathway and major regulatory inputs around hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase.
Slide 6. Aerobic versus anaerobic glycolysis: pyruvate can support mitochondrial oxidation when oxygen is available or be reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺. The slide also lists causes and symptoms of lactic acidosis.
Anaerobic purpose
Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue when mitochondrial oxidation cannot keep up or is unavailable.
Slide 7. Defective glycolysis can impair RBC deformability, producing echinocytes and extravascular hemolysis with anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and gallstones.
Slide 8. The RBC-specific 2,3-DPG pathway helps hemoglobin unload oxygen to tissues; fetal hemoglobin binds DPG poorly.
Slide 9. 2,3-BPG/DPG is placed within glycolysis and linked to right- versus left-shifting of the oxygen-hemoglobin curve.
Slide 10. The lecture compares major glycolytic enzyme deficiencies and their effects on hemolysis and oxygen affinity.
DefectLecture / aligned-note pattern
Pyruvate kinaseMost common glycolytic enzyme deficiency; hemolytic anemia; downstream block raises DPG → right shift.
HexokinaseSevere hemolytic anemia; early block reduces glycolytic output and DPG → left shift.
PFK-M / Tarui (GSD VII)Muscle glycogen-use defect with exercise intolerance/rhabdomyolysis plus RBC hemolysis; left shift in the lecture summary.

Slides 11–23: Glycogen, Hormones & Gluconeogenesis

Slide 12. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are presented as the two endogenous pathways that maintain blood glucose when dietary glucose is unavailable.
Slide 13. The liver changes direction with hormonal state: fed = high insulin/glucagon ratio and glucose storage; fasting = high glucagon/insulin ratio and glucose release.
Slide 17. Glycogenesis and glycogenolysis are placed on one map, emphasizing glycogen synthase for synthesis, phosphorylase/debranching enzyme for degradation, and liver glucose-6-phosphatase for free-glucose release.
Slide 18. Hormonal control table: glucagon acts in liver, insulin promotes storage, and epinephrine mobilizes glucose in liver and muscle.
Slide 19. Glucagon/epinephrine signaling through adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and PKA shifts glycogen metabolism toward degradation and away from synthesis.
Slide 20. The slide summarizes the phosphorylation-state logic: fasting/glucagon favors PKA-driven glycogen breakdown; fed/insulin favors PP1-mediated dephosphorylation and glycogen synthesis.
Slide 21. Skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase is activated by energy demand: AMP and contraction-associated Ca²⁺ reinforce glycogenolysis during exercise.
Slide 22. Cori and glucose-alanine cycles move lactate/alanine from muscle to liver, where carbon can be returned to blood as glucose through gluconeogenesis.
Slide 23. Gluconeogenesis bypasses irreversible glycolytic steps using glucose-6-phosphatase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, pyruvate carboxylase, and PEP carboxykinase. Deficiency leads to hypoglycemia with lactate accumulation/lactic acidosis.
Liver vs muscle
Liver has glucose-6-phosphatase → can export free glucose. Muscle lacks it → muscle glycogen is reserved for muscle ATP production.
Objective-supporting supplementary detail (not a core slide): the appended handout explains the ethanol objective. Ethanol metabolism raises hepatic NADH, limiting oxidized NAD⁺ needed to convert lactate→pyruvate and malate→oxaloacetate; in fasting, this compromises gluconeogenesis and can produce hypoglycemia with lactate accumulation. This is included only because the official objective explicitly names excess ethanol.

Slides 24–32: Glycogen Storage Diseases

Slide 24. GSDs result from abnormal glycogen synthesis or degradation. The lecture splits clinical patterns into fasting hypoglycemia/hepatomegaly versus exercise intolerance/muscle symptoms.
Slide 25. The lecture's comparison table organizes major GSDs by enzyme, organ affected, stored glycogen pattern, and clinical features.
Slide 26. Von Gierke disease is tied to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency and inability of liver to release free glucose.
Slide 28. McArdle disease is tied to muscle phosphorylase deficiency and failure of lactate to rise normally with exercise; rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria are highlighted.
Slide 29. The glycogen pathway map locates Von Gierke, Hers, McArdle, Cori, and Andersen defects at their respective steps.
Slide 30. The lecture table highlights lysosomal α-1,4-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe) and shows enzyme-replacement imagery.
Slide 31. The lecture table highlights phosphofructokinase deficiency in muscle (Tarui / GSD VII).
Slide 32. Tarui disease is placed at the PFK-M step: muscle symptoms resemble McArdle disease and RBC involvement adds hemolysis.
TypeDefectHigh-yield lecture pattern
I — Von GierkeGlucose-6-phosphataseSevere fasting hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly; cannot release free glucose from liver.
II — PompeLysosomal α-1,4-glucosidaseLysosomal glycogen accumulation; prominent muscle/heart involvement.
III — CoriDebranching enzymeLimit-dextrin / short-branch abnormal glycogen; liver + muscle pattern.
IV — AndersenBranching enzymeAbnormally long chains; progressive liver disease/cirrhosis.
V — McArdleMuscle glycogen phosphorylaseExercise intolerance, cramps, rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria; poor lactate rise.
VI — HersLiver glycogen phosphorylaseGenerally mild liver-predominant disease with hepatomegaly.
VII — TaruiMuscle PFKExercise intolerance/rhabdomyolysis plus hemolysis.

Last 60 Seconds

RBCs rely on glycolysis • LDH regenerates NAD⁺ • DPG right-shifts Hb and HbF binds DPG poorly • fed = insulin/storage • fasting = glucagon/release • liver has G6-phosphatase, muscle does not • glycogen synthase builds, phosphorylase breaks • ethanol can block gluconeogenesis in fasting • know GSD I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII patterns.
